stories.title: Kasidi Pickering Signs with Texas Tech — Portal's Biggest Bat Lands in Lubbock
stories.angle: All-American infielder Kasidi Pickering, who spent three seasons at Oklahoma and was one of the most coveted names in the transfer portal, has officially signed with Texas Tech. Pickering (.384 career BA, 50 HR, 169 RBI over three seasons at OU) adds firepower to a Red Raiders program already bolstered by Jaysoni Beachum (FSU transfer) under new coaches Cottrill and Pendley. TTU's portal class is now arguably the nation's best.

facebook.long_form:
It's official: Kasidi Pickering is a Texas Tech Red Raider.

The three-year Oklahoma All-American — who posted a .384 career batting average with 50 home runs and 169 RBI in Norman — has signed with the Red Raiders, confirming what has been building for weeks in the transfer portal.

Pickering's arrival in Lubbock is a landmark moment for a Texas Tech program that's been completely remade since coaches Cottrill and Pendley took over in 2026. The Red Raiders have assembled what many consider the nation's top portal class, adding Pickering alongside Jaysoni Beachum (Florida State IF) and Moriah Polar (Purdue batting average leader).

For OU fans, this stings. Pickering was a homegrown Big 12 talent who chose to leave after three seasons — and chose a Big 12 rival. For the sport, her move is a reminder of just how dramatically the transfer portal has changed the college softball landscape.

Oklahoma enters the spring with roster holes to fill. Texas Tech enters the spring as a contender. The Big 12 race just got a lot more unpredictable.

The 2028 contact window closed Sunday. What happens next is what matters.

Coaches spent October 17-18 calling, visiting, and evaluating prospects who won't set foot on a college campus for nearly three years. Now those conversations are turning into commitments — and the wave is rolling.

Here's where the top programs stand right now:

🥎 Texas — Leading the class with Michaela Landers (No. 1 IF, TX Bombers Gold), Ainsley Morvan (22 HR), and a deep pool of Texas-based talent.

🥎 Florida — Kylie Holden (No. 2 overall) headlines one of the nation's most complete early classes. Ryann Harris, Kate Losh, and Brooklyn Evans round it out.

🥎 Tennessee — Five commits including Caelyn Campos (No. 4 overall) and pitcher Megan Kuiper. The Lady Vols are building on 2026 WCWS momentum.

🥎 Oklahoma — Five commits, including connections to the TX Bombers Gold program.

🥎 Oklahoma State — Peyton Cleary (top-100 IF, Liberty North MO) gives the Cowgirls their first 2028 building block.

The industry hit 1,000+ total commits since September 1. The early recruiting era isn't slowing down.

facebook.long_form:
Tennessee's fall ball season has one game left.

Friday, October 23 at Sherri Parker Lee Stadium, the Lady Vols host Lee University in their final fall contest. Head coach Karen Weekly has overseen what she calls the deepest pitching staff in program history — and the performances have backed that up.

Karlyn Pickens, the No. 1 overall pick in the Athletes Unlimited Softball League Draft, put up a 194 strikeout, 1.70 ERA season in 2026. Sage Mardjetko went 16-3 with a 1.26 ERA and earned NFCA All-American honors. The staff is experienced, deep, and entering the offseason with a full fall's worth of development.

The offense showed its teeth in September when Emma Clarke hit for the cycle — recording a home run, a triple, two doubles, and six RBI in a single game.

Tennessee heads into winter looking like one of the favorites to return to Oklahoma City in 2027. The fall has been a preview of what's coming. One game left. Then the work begins.

stories.title: The Early Recruiting Machine — How College Softball Changed in Two Years
stories.angle: Since September 1, more than 1,000 softball players have committed to college programs. The 2028 contact window just closed — for eighth- and ninth-graders. The landscape has transformed dramatically since the NCAA adjusted contact rules, and programs like Texas, Oklahoma, Florida, and Tennessee are building powerhouses years before their recruits pick up a college glove. An explainer on the early recruiting era and what it means for players, families, and programs.

x_posts.label: Post 5
x_posts.text:
Oklahoma State just got its first Class of 2028 commit.

She's in 8th grade.

The early recruiting era in college softball isn't coming — it's already here. 1,000+ commits since September 1 tells you everything you need to know. 🥎

facebook.long_form:
Oklahoma State just got its first commitment from the Class of 2028.

The prospect — Peyton Cleary, a top-100 infielder from Liberty North High School in Missouri — is in eighth grade.

That's the reality of college softball recruiting in 2026. Since September 1, more than 1,000 players across the country have committed to college programs. The October 17-18 contact window — which allowed coaches to call prospects directly for the first time — was just the most recent marker in an acceleration that has been building for years.

How did we get here? A combination of factors: increased roster competition pushing programs to recruit earlier, rule changes that opened up earlier contact, and a cultural shift among elite programs that has made the "get them early" philosophy standard practice. Programs at Texas, Oklahoma, Florida, and Tennessee now regularly sign players who are still learning to drive.

For families of talented players, this creates both opportunity and pressure. The exposure circuit — travel ball, showcases, camps — has become a year-round operation.

It's a system that rewards early development and early decisions. Whether that's good for the sport long-term is a conversation worth having. For now, the numbers speak for themselves: 1,000+ commits, and counting.
